_doc: Built per EXAM-REVISION.md. Every bank item cites `src` into revision/sources/roshan/. Starting subjects: Science, History, Geography (English, Core Maths, PDHPE, Commerce, Food Tech to follow — formats noted below).

sections.name: Part A — Chemistry of New Substances

bank.ask: Name the FOUR indicators that a chemical change has taken place.
bank.model: Colour change; a gas produced (bubbles/fizzing); a precipitate forms; a temperature change (heat or light). (A new smell is also accepted.)

bank.ask: Classify each as a PHYSICAL or CHEMICAL change: (i) dissolving sugar (ii) burning paper (iii) boiling water.
bank.model: Dissolving sugar = physical; burning paper = chemical; boiling water = physical.

bank.ask: Write the word equation: when magnesium is heated in oxygen it forms magnesium oxide. Label the reactants and the product.
bank.model: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide. Reactants (left): magnesium, oxygen. Product (right): magnesium oxide.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part A Q4; Extract §SCIENCE model answer 1
bank.ask: State the Law of Conservation of Mass. A scientist runs the same reaction once in a closed jar and once in an open beaker and gets different masses. Why?
bank.model: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so mass of reactants = mass of products. In the closed jar no gas escapes so mass stays constant; in the open beaker a gas product escapes into the air, so the measured mass drops. Mass is still conserved.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part A Q5a (answer 49.6 g)
bank.ask: Hydrogen and oxygen react to form water. What mass of water forms if 14.8 g of hydrogen reacts with 34.8 g of oxygen? Show working.
bank.model: Mass of products = mass of reactants = 14.8 + 34.8 = 49.6 g of water.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part A Q5b (answer 1 g)
bank.ask: 10 g of magnesium is placed in 15 g of hydrochloric acid and hydrogen gas is produced. The solution then weighs 24 g. How many grams of hydrogen gas were released? Show working.
bank.model: Start = 10 + 15 = 25 g. 25 - 24 = 1 g of hydrogen gas escaped.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part A Q7; Extract §SCIENCE model answer 2 (elephant's toothpaste)
bank.ask: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2). What TYPE of reaction is this and how do you know? (Apply the definition.)
bank.model: Decomposition: one reactant breaks down into two or more products (AB -> A + B). Hydrogen peroxide (one reactant) breaks into water and oxygen (two products), so it is decomposition.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part A Q8; Extract §SCIENCE (corrosion)
bank.ask: (a) What conditions are needed for iron to rust? (b) Write the word equation. (c) Give TWO ways to prevent rusting.
bank.model: (a) Iron + oxygen + water (all three needed). (b) iron + oxygen + water -> hydrated iron oxide (rust). (c) Any two: paint it; oil/grease/plastic-coat it; galvanise with zinc; use a sacrificial metal; keep it dry.

bank.ask: Identify the bonding in each: MgF2 (metal + non-metal), CO2 (two non-metals), Cu (a metal).
bank.model: MgF2 = ionic (metal + non-metal); CO2 = covalent (two non-metals); Cu = metallic (a metal).

bank.ask: Compare covalent and ionic bonding — the elements involved, what happens to the electrons, the structures formed, with an example of each.
bank.model: Both fill their outer electron shells for stability. Covalent bonding is between non-metals that SHARE electrons, forming individual molecules (e.g. H2O, CO2, O2). Ionic bonding is between a metal and a non-metal that TRANSFER electrons, forming lattices of charged ions (e.g. NaCl, CaCO3).

bank.ask: Soluble or insoluble? (i) barium sulfate (ii) potassium chloride (iii) aluminium hydroxide.
bank.model: Barium sulfate = insoluble; potassium chloride = soluble; aluminium hydroxide = insoluble. (Nitrates and group-1 salts dissolve; most carbonates/hydroxides and barium/lead sulfates are insoluble.)

bank.ask: Lithium carbonate + barium nitrate react. (a) Name the two products. (b) Which product is the insoluble precipitate?
bank.model: (a) barium carbonate + lithium nitrate. (b) Barium carbonate is the precipitate (carbonates are insoluble except group 1); lithium nitrate stays dissolved.

bank.src: Extract §SCIENCE model answer (Wegener); Study Pack §1 Part B Q
bank.ask: Describe the Theory of Continental Drift, the evidence Alfred Wegener used, and explain why other scientists dismissed it at the time.
bank.model: Continents were once joined and have drifted apart. Wegener saw the continents fit like a jigsaw and collected evidence of matching rock types, mountain formations and fossils across continents now separated by oceans, proposing a supercontinent (Pangaea). But he was not a geologist and could not explain HOW continents move (the mechanism), so his theory was dismissed.

bank.ask: Distinguish between a convergent and a divergent plate boundary — the movement, what happens to the crust, and the features formed at each.
bank.model: Convergent: plates move towards each other; continental crust compresses or oceanic crust subducts, forming mountain ranges, trenches or volcanic islands. Divergent: plates move apart; continental crust rifts or magma rises to form new oceanic crust, forming mid-ocean ridges.

bank.ask: Which plate boundaries are most linked to volcanoes, and name ONE hazard an earthquake can cause.
bank.model: Volcanoes are most linked to convergent and divergent boundaries. An earthquake hazard: ground shaking, building collapse, tsunamis, landslides or fires (any one).

bank.ask: Compare oceanic and continental crust (thickness, density, age).
bank.model: Oceanic crust is thinner, denser and younger (basalt); continental crust is thicker, less dense and older (granite). Oceanic crust subducts under continental crust.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part B calculation (answer 1.3 cm/yr)
bank.ask: A strip of seafloor basalt is 72,000,000 years old and 936 km from the mid-ocean ridge. (a) Convert the distance to cm. (b) Calculate the spreading rate in cm/year. Show working. (1 km = 100,000 cm)
Why do ocean-floor rocks get older the further they are from a mid-ocean ridge?
bank.model: New crust forms at the ridge (youngest there) and seafloor spreading pushes it outwards, so rock further away was made longer ago and is older.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part C Skills list; Extract §SCIENCE (variables)
bank.ask: A student investigates whether warmer water makes sugar dissolve faster. (a) Write a hypothesis in the 'If... then...' form. (b) State the independent and dependent variables. (c) Name TWO controlled variables.
bank.model: (a) If the water temperature is increased, then the sugar dissolves faster. (b) Independent = water temperature; dependent = time taken to dissolve. (c) Any two: mass of sugar, volume of water, stirring, type of sugar.

bank.ask: What is the difference between the RELIABILITY and the VALIDITY of an experiment?
bank.model: Reliability = repeating the experiment (at least 3 times) to get consistent results. Validity = a fair test that measures what it is meant to, with only the independent variable changed.

bank.src: Study Pack §1 Part C (describing trends — must mention both variables; interpolating)
bank.ask: A reaction's temperature over time: Time(s) 0,10,20,30,40 -> Temp(C) 20,26,31,34,35. (a) Name the independent variable. (b) Describe the trend, mentioning BOTH variables. (c) Estimate the temperature at 25 s.
bank.model: (a) Time. (b) As time increased, temperature increased, but the rate of increase slowed and levelled off near 35 C. (c) About 32-33 C (interpolating between 31 and 34).

bank.ask: Give TWO reasons why Japan attacked Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941.
bank.model: Any two: to cripple the US Pacific Fleet so it could not stop Japanese expansion; to secure resources (e.g. oil) and territory across South-East Asia and the Pacific; in response to US sanctions / the oil embargo.

bank.src: Study Pack §2 Topic 2; Extract §HISTORY (Fall of Singapore)
bank.ask: Explain how the threat of Japanese expansion changed Australia's sense of security in 1942, and how the government used propaganda posters (e.g. 'He's Coming South') to shape public feeling.
bank.model: The fall of Singapore (Feb 1942), a major British base, shattered Australia's security and shifted its alliance towards the USA. With Japan advancing south and Darwin bombed, Australians feared invasion. Posters such as 'He's Coming South' and 'Ringed with Menace' created panic and urgency, pushing people to enlist, work and support the war.

bank.ask: Describe what happened to ONE of the forces sent to defend Australia's north (Lark Force at Rabaul, Gull Force at Ambon, or Sparrow Force at Timor): who they were, what happened, and the outcome.
bank.model: e.g. Gull Force (Ambon): ~1,100 troops sent to defend Laha airfield; Japan invaded 30 Jan 1942 and they surrendered 3 Feb. In the Laha Massacre 300+ POWs were killed; the rest suffered starvation and disease at Tan Toey and nearly 80% died in captivity. (Lark Force/Montevideo Maru, or Sparrow Force's guerrilla war, also valid.)

bank.src: Study Pack §2 Topic 4; Extract §HISTORY (POW camps / Geneva)
bank.ask: Did the Japanese treat POWs in accordance with the 1929 Geneva Convention? Justify your answer with at least TWO Geneva standards and evidence from the Thai-Burma Railway.
bank.model: No. The Convention required humane treatment, adequate food/shelter/medical care, safe non-military work and protection from arbitrary punishment. The Japanese breached these: watery-rice rations, up-to-18-hour 'Speedo' shifts, beatings (68 men beaten to death at Hellfire Pass) and little medical care, leading to 16,000+ POW deaths.

bank.ask: The death rate in Japanese POW camps was about 27% vs about 4% in German/Italian camps. Give ONE reason why.
bank.model: The Japanese did not follow the Geneva Convention — starvation, forced labour, brutal beatings and disease with little medical care caused far more deaths.

bank.ask: Give TWO facts about the Thai-Burma ('Death') Railway (e.g. length, route, number of Australians, a named location).
bank.model: Any two: ~415 km long; ran Ban Pong (Thailand) to Thanbyuzayat (Burma); ~13,000 of ~60,000 Allied POWs were Australian; included 'Hellfire Pass'; 2,800+ Australians died building it.

bank.ask: Describe a major challenge Australian POWs faced on the Thai-Burma Railway. Use the scaffold: challenge -> effect -> specific example -> impact.
bank.model: Starvation and tropical disease: tiny watery-rice rations and little clean water left men too weak to fight off cholera, dysentery and malaria. Exemplified by the 1943 'Speedo' with 18-hour shifts; F Force suffered ~44% deaths. Impact: 16,000+ Allied POWs died, 2,800+ Australians.

bank.ask: Why did the Japanese build the Thai-Burma Railway instead of supplying by sea?
bank.model: Shipping by sea had become too dangerous (especially after Midway), so the railway gave a safer overland supply route into Burma.

bank.ask: When was Darwin first bombed, and why was it significant for Australia?
bank.model: 19 February 1942. Significant because it was the first attack on the Australian mainland, it shocked the nation and showed Australia was directly under threat.

bank.src: Study Pack §2 Topic 7; Extract §HISTORY (Kokoda model paragraph)
bank.ask: Describe a significant challenge Australian and Papuan soldiers faced on the Kokoda Trail. Use the scaffold: challenge -> effect -> example -> impact.
bank.model: Extreme mountain terrain: steep, muddy ridges and dense jungle exhausted the troops and made moving food and medical supplies nearly impossible. Exemplified by the climbs over the Owen Stanley Range, causing severe shortages. Impact: high casualties as units could not be supplied or wounded evacuated.

bank.ask: Why was the Kokoda campaign important for Australia?
bank.model: Australian and Papuan troops halted the Japanese advance towards Port Moresby, helping protect Australia from invasion — a crucial defensive victory in brutal conditions.

bank.ask: On the Kokoda Trail, who were the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels' and what did they do?
bank.model: Papuan (New Guinean) carriers who carried supplies and wounded soldiers over the difficult terrain and cared for the injured.

bank.src: Study Pack §2 Topic 8; Extract §HISTORY (Indigenous service — stated on exam)
bank.ask: Name ONE way the WWII service of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people was restricted or treated differently from other Australians.
bank.model: Any one: restrictions on enlisting; serving in segregated units; discrimination; or being denied the same recognition, pay or benefits as other veterans after the war.

exam.src: Study Pack §3 (Format 30 marks: Section I MC 10, Section II short 20)

bank.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I Q1 (ans b)
bank.ask: Which statement best defines economic restructuring?
opts: Growth of primary industries and agriculture
Shift from manufacturing to service and knowledge-based economies
Movement of people from urban to rural areas
bank.e: Economic restructuring = shift from manufacturing towards service/knowledge industries.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I Q5 (ans c)
bank.ask: Which is NOT an issue of over-urbanisation in the Global South?
bank.e: High-tech service economies are a Global North feature, not an over-urbanisation issue.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I Q7 (ans a)
bank.ask: Between 2001 and 2024 Dee Why's median rent went from $220 to $740/week. This reflects:
bank.e: Rising rents reflect gentrification and housing pressure.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I Q9 (ans b)
bank.ask: Which strategy most directly reduces stormwater runoff and coastal erosion?
bank.e: WSUD captures, treats and reuses stormwater, reducing runoff and erosion.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I Q10 (ans a)
bank.ask: Despite renewal, Pittwater Rd traffic rose 21% (2015-2023). This shows:
opts: A complete shift to active transport
bank.e: Rising traffic shows continued car dependence despite walkability efforts.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 data skills Q1 (ans b, 236%)
bank.ask: Rate of change (%) = (new - old) / old x 100. Dee Why's median rent rose from $220 to $740. The % increase is closest to:

bank.src: Study Pack §3 data skills Q2 (ans a, 184%)
bank.ask: Median weekly household income rose from $930 to $2,640. The % increase is closest to:
Define 'liveability'.
bank.model: Liveability refers to the quality of life experienced by people in a place, based on environmental, social and economic factors.

bank.ask: Define 'urban consolidation'.
bank.model: Increasing population density within existing urban areas through higher-density housing (apartments, townhouses, infill) to reduce urban sprawl and use infrastructure efficiently.

bank.ask: Define 'gentrification'.
bank.model: The process by which higher-income residents and businesses move into previously lower-income urban areas, raising property values and transforming the social character of the place.

bank.topic: Why Dee Why was renewed (4 marks)
bank.src: Study Pack §3 Section II Q11; Extract §GEOGRAPHY (drivers)
bank.ask: Explain why Dee Why underwent urban renewal. Give at least TWO reasons. (4 marks)
bank.model: Sydney's growth and the Metropolis of Three Cities plan pushed for higher density to reduce sprawl; Dee Why's rising land value made redevelopment viable; it was already a central, established Northern Beaches hub; and parts of the town centre had decayed, making it ripe for renewal.

bank.src: Study Pack §3 Section II Q13; Extract §GEOGRAPHY (environmental sustainability)
bank.ask: Assess how effective WSUD and increased tree canopy have been for Dee Why's environmental sustainability. Use evidence and include ONE limitation. (6 marks)
bank.model: Moderately effective. WSUD restored the lagoon/dunes, grew beach width ~11 m and improved water quality (WQI 80/100); tree canopy rose 15%->23%, each 10% gain lowering temperature ~1 C. Limitation: 70% of canopy gain was public land while private fell 6%, drains blocked in the 2023 storms, and Pittwater Rd traffic rose 21%.

bank.src: Extract §GEOGRAPHY (model evaluation); Study Pack §3 Section III Q16
bank.ask: Evaluate the extent to which urban renewal has improved overall liveability in Dee Why. Use at least THREE indicators, give a clear judgement, support with evidence. (8 marks)
bank.model: Renewal driven by gentrification raised apartment investment but escalated prices/rents — median unit $340k (2001) -> $1.11m (2024), renters in stress +19%. Transport (B-Line) and canopy (15%->23%) improved, but overall liveability declined as renewal prioritised profit over affordability. Judgement: moderate gains to economic/environmental liveability, but reduced social liveability through unaffordability.

bank.ask: Name the THREE cities in the NSW 'Metropolis of Three Cities' plan for Greater Sydney.
bank.model: Eastern Harbour City (Sydney CBD), Central River City (Parramatta), Western Parkland City (around the new Western Sydney Airport).

bank.src: Extract §GEOGRAPHY (rate of change; rent +236% vs income +184%)
bank.ask: Dee Why's income rose from $930 to $2,640 and rent from $220 to $740. Which rose by a greater percentage, and what does that mean for affordability?
bank.model: Rent rose ~236% vs income ~184%, so rent rose faster than income. Affordability declined and rental stress increased.
